title: A Bad Outcome Can Still Be Stable
everyday_situation: Two coworkers both stay quiet about a broken process because each one expects the other to stay quiet too. Speaking alone is costly, so silence continues.
mistaken_reading: The easy mistake is to say the bad process survives because people do not understand it is bad.
first_principles_correction: Game theory asks whether speaking is individually worth it given what each person expects the others to do. A bad group outcome can persist when no one person has a safe move away.
why_it_matters: This changes the fix. More explanation may not solve the problem. The setting may need protection for speaking up, shared commitment, or a rule that changes the payoff from moving first.
where_else_it_applies: Coordination failures, public goods, price competition, voting, workplace silence, and technology standards all use this same stability-versus-goodness distinction.

title: A Threat Is Not Real Until The Future Incentive Works
everyday_situation: A manager says they will punish missed deadlines, but everyone knows the punishment would also delay the manager's own project.
mistaken_reading: The easy mistake is to treat the announcement as enough. The words sound serious, so the threat is assumed to work.
first_principles_correction: Sequential reasoning checks the later moment. If the manager would not want to carry out the punishment later, the threat may not shape behavior now.
why_it_matters: This changes the design. A credible rule needs automatic consequences, reputation costs, outside enforcement, or a later payoff that makes follow-through worthwhile.
where_else_it_applies: Entry deterrence, bargaining, international threats, platform moderation, legal penalties, and repeated relationships all depend on later incentives.

title: Hidden Information Changes What Actions Mean
everyday_situation: A seller offers a warranty. The buyer asks whether the warranty is a real sign of quality or just a cheap promise anyone would make.
mistaken_reading: The easy mistake is to treat the action as proof by itself.
first_principles_correction: The action is evidence only if different hidden types face different incentives. If low-quality sellers can copy the warranty cheaply, the warranty may not separate types.
why_it_matters: This changes how the buyer reads the market. The right question is not whether the signal sounds reassuring, but whether the wrong type would find it too costly or unattractive to imitate.
where_else_it_applies: Education signals, product warranties, online badges, security deposits, reviews, insurance menus, and hiring screens all use this same logic.

title: A Rule Changes What A Choice Means
everyday_situation: Two platforms both ask advertisers for bids, but one charges the winner's own bid while another uses a different payment rule.
mistaken_reading: The easy mistake is to compare bids as if a bid always means the same thing.
first_principles_correction: A bid is read through the allocation and payment rule. The same advertiser may bid differently when the cost of winning changes.
why_it_matters: This changes how a platform should be evaluated. Revenue, truthfulness, user quality, advertiser learning, and budget pacing depend on the rule, not only on bidder values.
where_else_it_applies: Auctions, school choice, procurement, platform ranking, matching, ad markets, and contract menus all show how rule design changes incentives.

title: The Future Can Discipline The Present
everyday_situation: A seller could cheat one customer today, but doing so may destroy repeat business and public reputation tomorrow.
mistaken_reading: The easy mistake is to say trust appears because the seller is nice or disappears because the seller is selfish.
first_principles_correction: Repeated-game reasoning compares the short-run gain from cheating with the future loss from punishment, lost trust, or broken relationships.
why_it_matters: This changes what evidence to look for. You need patience, observation, punishment capacity, and enough future value. Without those pieces, repetition may not support cooperation.
where_else_it_applies: Implicit cartels, workplace trust, long-term contracting, online reputation, diplomacy, and community enforcement all rely on future consequences.

title: Publicness Can Matter More Than New Information
everyday_situation: Everyone privately suspects a meeting has moved, but no one wants to act until there is a public announcement.
mistaken_reading: The easy mistake is to say the announcement adds no information because people already suspected the fact.
first_principles_correction: The public announcement changes what each person can expect others to know and rely on. That shared confidence can change coordination.
why_it_matters: This changes communication design. Sometimes the important feature is not the content of the message but whether everyone knows that everyone received it.
where_else_it_applies: Public policy, standards, protests, bank runs, platform rule changes, voting, and classroom coordination all depend on shared awareness.

title: Existence Is Not Prediction
everyday_situation: A theorem says an equilibrium exists, but a reader still does not know which one people will reach or whether it is good.
mistaken_reading: The easy mistake is to treat existence as if the real world must find that point.
first_principles_correction: Fixed-point reasoning can prove the model has a stable point under assumptions. It does not by itself prove uniqueness, learning, computation, welfare, or empirical relevance.
why_it_matters: This changes how mathematical results are used. Existence makes the model coherent, but the reader still has to ask how the point is selected and whether the assumptions match the setting.
where_else_it_applies: Nash existence, mixed strategies, matching, platform equilibria, network games, and algorithmic game theory all separate existence from computation and selection.

title: The Payoff Choice Carries The Moral And Practical Burden
everyday_situation: A policy model gives one score to each outcome, but the people affected care about money, risk, fairness, dignity, and future options.
mistaken_reading: The easy mistake is to accept the score because it makes the model solvable.
first_principles_correction: A payoff is a chosen comparison tool. If it leaves out a real pressure, the later equilibrium or design result may optimize the wrong object.
why_it_matters: This changes criticism. Instead of saying the model is unrealistic in general, the reader can ask exactly which value, cost, risk, or outside harm was left out.
where_else_it_applies: Welfare analysis, platform objectives, auctions, bargaining, public policy, employment models, and algorithmic scoring all depend on what the payoff counts.
